notes:
# Joshua 14 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

## Verses 1–2: The Administrators and Method of Distribution

**v. 1 — "Now these are the portions that the Israelites inherited in the land of Canaan, as distributed by Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the heads of the families of the tribes of Israel."**

- **Ellicott** notes the careful order: Eleazar is named *before* Joshua, in strict accordance with Numbers 27:21, where the priest held legislative authority while Joshua held executive power. "Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun were the rulers" — the priest and judge together form the Mosaic constitutional government until a king arose. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-14.html)

- **Gill** observes that the "heads of the fathers" were the ten princes, one from each tribe, who had been appointed by name through Moses seven years earlier (Numbers 34:17) to oversee this very task. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-14.html)

- **Precept Austin** (citing Dale Ralph Davis) notes the literary structure: "This section opens and closes with the two faithful spies (see Num. 13–14) receiving their respective inheritances, Caleb in 14:6–15 and Joshua in 19:49–50." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-14-commentary)

- **Guzik / Enduring Word** stresses that these lands were gained by conquest yet in a greater sense by *inheritance*, because God had promised the land by covenant to Abraham's descendants (Genesis 13:15; 17:8). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-14/)

---

**v. 2 — "Their inheritance was assigned by lot for the nine and a half tribes, as the LORD had commanded through Moses."**

- **Gill** explains that the lot was used to prevent future quarrels and to demonstrate that the distribution came from God's providence, not human decision. He adds a typological note: "In this Canaan was a type of the heavenly inheritance, which the saints obtain by lot, in and through Christ, the antitypical Joshua, Ephesians 1:11." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-14.html)

- **Guzik** relays an ancient rabbinic tradition (via Ginzberg) about how the lots worked: the land was divided into ten provinces, numbered; ten pieces with numbers and ten with tribal names were placed in two containers; Joshua drew from one, Eleazar from the other. This honoured God's sovereignty (Proverbs 16:33). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-14/)

---

## Verses 3–5: Why Nine and a Half Tribes (Not Twelve)

**v. 3 — "For Moses had given the inheritance east of the Jordan to the other two and a half tribes. But he granted no inheritance among them to the Levites."**

- **Gill** notes that the exclusion of Levi is "frequently observed, that it might be taken notice of, to show the disinterestedness of Moses in this affair, Levi being his own tribe; and to recommend the care of the Levites to the other tribes." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-14.html)

---

**v. 4 — "The descendants of Joseph became two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim. And no portion of the land was given to the Levites, except for cities in which to live, along with pasturelands for their flocks and herds."**

- **Gill** explains the "double portion" logic: Reuben forfeited the birthright (through sin), and it passed to Joseph, whose two sons each became a full tribe. This kept the number of landed tribes at twelve despite Levi having no territorial inheritance. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-14.html)

- **Ellicott** adds a fascinating observation about the high priest's garments reflecting this double count: on the shoulders, the names were "according to their birth" (Joseph included, Ephraim and Manasseh omitted); on the breastplate, they were "according to the twelve tribes" (Ephraim and Manasseh listed, Joseph and Levi omitted). Both ways preserved the number twelve and emphasised it. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-14.html)

- **Guzik** notes simply: "We commonly think and speak of the 'twelve tribes of Israel' but there were thirteen." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-14/)

---

**v. 5 — "So the Israelites did as the LORD had commanded Moses, and they divided the land."**

- **Gill** clarifies that "they divided the land" means they met, prepared, and began the process; the actual division was not yet completed, and the following incident with Caleb occurs before the full distribution. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-14.html)

---

## Verses 6–9: Caleb Remembers Moses' Promise

**v. 6 — "Then the sons of Judah approached Joshua at Gilgal, and Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite said to him, 'You know what the LORD said to Moses the man of God at Kadesh-barnea about you and me.'"**

- **Gill** notes that "the children of Judah" were not the whole tribe but "some of the chief men of it who accompanied Caleb, for the honour of him … he being their prince; and to second his petition." Caleb speaks alone because the matter concerns him personally. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-14.html)

- **Ellicott** highlights a contrast of character: Caleb, a commissioner from Judah for dividing the land (Numbers 34:19), comes forward *first* to ask for his inheritance — but the post he requests is the most dangerous of all. "It is noticeable that of the two faithful spies whom Moses sent, Caleb received his inheritance first, and Joshua last of all Israel. (See Joshua 19:49.) The characters of the two men are well seen in this contrast—the one foremost in a service of danger; the other last to seek the things that were his own." Ellicott then draws a Christological parallel: "Thus, 'even Christ pleased not Himself' (comp. Joshua); but 'the reproaches of them that reproached thee fell on me,' as the conquest of the sons of Anak fell to the lot of Caleb." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-14.html)

- **Spurgeon** (preaching from Numbers 14:24 but referencing Caleb throughout) interprets Caleb's name as "all heart": "Here was a fitting surname for the man, whose whole heart followed his God." The alternative meaning "dog" also carries virtue: "never dog so followed his master as Caleb followed his God." (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/caleb-the-man-for-the-times)

- **The Pulpit Commentary Homiletics** (R. Glover) notes that the epithet "Kenizzite" has led many to conclude "with considerable probability, that Caleb was a proselyte" — a foreigner (perhaps from Midian or Edom) who threw in his lot with Israel. This makes his wholehearted devotion all the more remarkable. (https://biblehub.com/sermons/joshua/14-13.htm)

- **Guzik** adds that Caleb addresses Moses as "the man of God" — a term of deep respect and veneration. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-14/)

---

**v. 7 — "I was forty years old when Moses the servant of the LORD sent me from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land, and I brought back to him an honest report."**

- **Gill:** Caleb gave "a sincere, honest and faithful representation of the land, and its inhabitants, as it appeared to him." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-14.html)

- **Ellicott** uses the age data here (along with v.10) to calculate the duration of the conquest: Caleb was 40 at the spying (second year of the Exodus), approximately 78 at the Jordan crossing (38½ years later), and 85 when the land division began. "Therefore the conquest itself must have extended over a period of seven years." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-14.html)

- The **Ligonier** devotional (Reformed) notes that Caleb "brought back word as it was in my heart" — his honest report flowed from an inner integrity and trust in God. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/faithfulness-rewarded)

---

**v. 8 — "Although my brothers who went with me made the hearts of the people melt with fear, I remained loyal to the LORD my God."**

- **Gill:** "made the heart of the people melt" means they "discouraged them, filled them with fears, sunk their spirits, that their hearts flowed, and became as weak as water." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-14.html)

- **Whedon's Commentary** explains "heart…melt" as meaning fear, not compassion (the older sense of the phrase). He connects "wholly followed" to the events of Numbers 14:6–10: "There no treachery of their brethren the fellow-spies, no panic of their own, no fury of the people, could disturb the calmness of their witness for God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/joshua-14.html)

- **Guzik** notes that only three people in Scripture are described as having "wholly followed the LORD": Caleb, Joshua (Numbers 32:11–12), and David (1 Kings 11:6). This phrase "seems to have made a significant impression on him" since Caleb repeats it twice. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-14/)

---

**v. 9 — "On that day Moses swore to me, saying, 'Surely the land on which you have set foot will be an inheritance to you and your children forever, because you have wholly followed the LORD my God.'"**

- **Gill** clarifies: "Moses sware" means Moses "declared the oath of the Lord, for it was the Lord that sware" (Deut 1:34). The specific promise of Hebron is not recorded verbatim in Numbers or Deuteronomy, but Gill notes that "it was understood and known to be the meaning of it" — and Numbers 13:22 says "*he* [singular] came to Hebron," which Jewish tradition understands as Caleb alone. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-14.html)

- **Ellicott** is more cautious: "Whether Moses referred to Hebron specifically in this promise, it is impossible to say." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-14.html)

- **Kretzmann's Commentary** (Lutheran) notes: "This account supplements that given Numbers 14, for it can be understood only of a direct promise made to Caleb, with special reference to Hebron and its vicinity, where the giants lived who had so terrified the other spies." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/joshua-14.html)

---

## Verses 10–12: Caleb's Bold Request

**v. 10 — "Now behold, as the LORD promised, He has kept me alive these forty-five years since He spoke this word to Moses, while Israel wandered in the wilderness. So here I am today, eighty-five years old."**

- **Guzik** notes that Caleb's preservation was remarkable not only because of battles and advanced age but "because only he and Joshua were spared the judgment of death that fell upon all the generation of adults who left Egypt, the generation of unbelief." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-14/)

- **The Bible.org sermon** (Evangelical) emphasises Caleb's refusal to grow bitter: "He is receiving the inheritance that God through Moses had promised him so many years before without any indication of bitterness for having to wait so long, no evidence of rebellion or anger, no 'where-were-you-God-when-I-needed-you.'" (https://bible.org/seriespage/8-caleb-finishing-strong-josh-146-15)

- **Ellicott** calculates that Caleb was about 78 at the Jordan crossing, confirming the conquest wars lasted roughly seven years. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-14.html)

---

**v. 11 — "still as strong today as I was the day Moses sent me out. As my strength was then, so it is now for war, for going out, and for coming in."**

- **Ellicott** contrasts Caleb's preserved vigour with Joshua's aging (Joshua 13:1): "Yet Joshua died at the age of 110, only 25 years older than Caleb was at this time. They were contemporaries. But the far greater responsibility lying upon Joshua (with a possible difference of temperament) may very naturally account for the one man's having aged so much more rapidly than the other." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-14.html)

- **Guzik** notes the three spheres of Caleb's ongoing strength: "for war" (military combat), "for going out" (daily business and leadership), and "for coming in" (home life and ordinary routines). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-14/)

- The **Ligonier** devotional (Reformed) adds: "So gracious has God been to Caleb that he is as strong at 85 as at 40." This is attributed to God's preserving hand. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/faithfulness-rewarded)

---

**v. 12 — "Now therefore give me this hill country that the LORD promised me on that day, for you yourself heard then that the Anakim were there, with great and fortified cities. Perhaps with the LORD's help I will drive them out, as the LORD has spoken."**

- **Guzik** highlights that Caleb "wanted the fight, practically demanding the mountain where difficult foes lived. He could have asked for an easy place, but he knew these foes must be faced and thought that he may as well be the one to do it." At 85, he didn't leave the hard work to younger men. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-14/)

- **The Ligonier devotional** quotes Matthew Henry: "We may suppose that Caleb, observing what stress [the spies] laid upon the difficulty of conquering Hebron, a city garrisoned by the giants … bravely desired to have that city which they called invincible assigned to himself." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/faithfulness-rewarded)

- **Kretzmann's (Lutheran) Commentary** explains that Joshua had previously conquered these cities during his campaigns (Joshua 11:21), but had not garrisoned them, so the Anakim had returned and resettled. Caleb must now drive them out again. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/joshua-14.html)

- **Gill** notes the phrase "if so be the Lord will be with me" (KJV) or "perhaps with the LORD's help": Caleb "relied upon the promise of God to enable him to do this, and not upon his natural strength and courage, or the number and prowess of the warlike tribe of Judah." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-14.html)

- **Spurgeon** (in a related sermon on Judges 1:19–20) says: "Caleb, that grand old man … went up in his old age, when his bones were sore and set, and slew the three sons of Anak, even three mighty giants, and took possession of their city. In this way the Lord's power was trusted and vindicated." (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/chariots-of-iron)

- **Bible.org** (Evangelical) emphasises that Caleb's "perhaps" is not doubt but humble dependence: "He was fully confident in the Lord's presence. He was fully dependent on the Lord's power. He was fully trusting in the Lord's promise." (https://bible.org/seriespage/8-caleb-finishing-strong-josh-146-15)

---

## Verses 13–15: Joshua Grants Caleb's Request

**v. 13 — "Then Joshua blessed Caleb son of Jephunneh and gave him Hebron as his inheritance."**

- **Guzik** explains: "This means that Joshua approved Caleb's request, praised him for the asking, and prayed that God's blessing would be on him in the endeavor to take Hebron and its area." The blessing was not mere approval but "a prayerful invocation of God's favour." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-14/)

- **Gill** clarifies an important geographic detail: "This is to be understood not of the city of Hebron itself, for that was given to the Levites, and was a city of refuge, but the country round about in the fields and villages annexed to it, as appears from Joshua 21:12." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-14.html)

- **The Pulpit Commentary Homiletics** (R. Glover) notes: "Joshua grants it, and the Lord gives it him. And the land which saw his courage became his inheritance for generations." He adds an application: "Godliness begets manliness of the noblest kind … By communion with God man attains calmness, wisdom, strength, and help." (https://biblehub.com/sermons/joshua/14-13.htm)

---

**v. 14 — "Therefore Hebron belongs to Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite as an inheritance to this day, because he wholly followed the LORD, the God of Israel."**

- **Guzik** observes that the phrase "because he wholly followed the LORD God of Israel" is repeated as the summary explanation of Caleb's reward. He adds: "If all Israel had the heart and faith of Caleb, their conquest of Canaan would have been much more complete." He connects this to the New Testament call to be "living sacrifices" (Romans 12:1–2). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-14/)

- The **Ligonier** devotional (Reformed) ties this to the broader theme of God's faithfulness: "Caleb can attest that God has kept His promise to preserve him through wilderness and war." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/faithfulness-rewarded)

- **Bible.org** notes that the phrase "to this day" shows the lasting nature of God's reward to faithfulness: "He finished strong in faith. If you had to write a title over Caleb's life, what would it be? I think it would be: He wholly followed the Lord." (https://bible.org/seriespage/8-caleb-finishing-strong-josh-146-15)

- **Gill** discusses "the Kenezite" — whether this title belonged to Caleb or his father Jephunneh, and whether it connects to Kenaz, a duke of Edom (Genesis 36:15). This reinforces the possibility that Caleb was a Gentile proselyte. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-14.html)

---

**v. 15 — "(Hebron used to be called Kiriath-arba, after Arba, the greatest man among the Anakim.) Then the land had rest from war."**

- **Ellicott** discusses the name "Kiriath-arba": "Arba means four in Hebrew, and therefore some have endeavoured to interpret it as the city of four." Rashi suggested it was "the city of Ahiman, and Sheshai, and Talmai, and their father." But Ellicott insists: "the text of Joshua seems to leave no doubt that Arba was a man's name." He notes the difficulty of whether Hebron was called Hebron before or after it was Kiriath-arba, given Genesis 23:2 refers to the place where Sarah died as Kiriath-arba. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-14.html)

- **Ellicott** also puzzles over the phrase "the land had rest from war," which appears earlier and more naturally in Joshua 11:23 as the close of the war narratives. Its reappearance here may be connected to the final dispossession of the Anakim by Caleb. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-14.html)

- **Bible.org** interprets this as a narrative summary: "It's as though the writer is saying, 'There was one more battle to be fought. One more war to be won. One more mountain to be taken. And Caleb did it. Then the land had rest from war.'" (https://bible.org/seriespage/8-caleb-finishing-strong-josh-146-15)

- **Guzik** simply notes that this rest from war was the fruit of Caleb's faithful conquest of the very region that had terrified the ten unfaithful spies forty-five years earlier. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-14/)

---

## Denominational Distinctives and Differing Emphases

Protestant traditions broadly agree on the meaning of Joshua 14, but their emphases differ:

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** Emphasises God's sovereign preservation of Caleb through the wilderness and warfare, and the reward of faithfulness as a display of God's covenant faithfulness. The application stresses studying the lives of faithful saints as a means of strengthening trust in God. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/faithfulness-rewarded)

- **Baptist (Spurgeon):** Focuses on Caleb's inner character — the "another spirit" within him (Numbers 14:24). Spurgeon unpacks "wholly followed" under four heads: universally (without dividing), sincerely (without dissembling), cheerfully (without disputing), and constantly (without declining). The sermon is intensely practical and evangelistic, pressing hearers toward wholehearted personal devotion. (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/caleb-the-man-for-the-times)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik):** Emphasises Caleb's bold faith, his physical vigour at 85 as a sign of God's blessing, and the practical principle that faith grows stronger with age. The application is strongly motivational: believers should ask for the "mountain" — the hardest challenge — and trust God for victory. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-14/)

- **Lutheran (Kretzmann's Commentary):** Takes a historically careful approach, explaining the narrative details (the Anakim had resettled Hebron after Joshua's earlier campaign), and emphasises that Caleb "wholly followed the Lord" by "having trusted faithfully in the almighty power of Jehovah." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/joshua-14.html)

- **Evangelical (Bible.org):** Stresses finishing strong in old age, perseverance through discouragement, and leaving a legacy of faith. The application is directed at the believer's lifelong faithfulness rather than at any particular doctrinal distinctive. (https://bible.org/seriespage/8-caleb-finishing-strong-josh-146-15)

---

## Other Views and Notable Points

**"Caleb the Kenizzite" — Was He a Gentile?**

The Pulpit Commentary Homiletics (R. Glover) and several older commentators raise the possibility that Caleb was a proselyte — a Gentile who joined Israel. The evidence: the persistent epithet "Kenizzite" (vv. 6, 14), the connection to Kenaz (a name among the "dukes of Edom," Genesis 36:15), and the phrasing of Joshua 15:13 which suggests Caleb was "settled amongst" Judah rather than being a native son. Glover writes: "One of those who, like Heber the Kenite, threw in his lot with Israel — perhaps a Midianitish youth who attached himself to Moses — and by force of faith, energy, and wisdom commended himself for any service of special difficulty." If correct, this makes Caleb an early example of a Gentile incorporated into the covenant people by faith. (https://biblehub.com/sermons/joshua/14-13.htm)

**Chronology of the Conquest**

Ellicott's calculation from Caleb's ages (40 at Kadesh-barnea, 85 at the land division) provides the only direct biblical evidence for the length of Joshua's wars: approximately seven years. This is widely accepted in traditional commentaries. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-14.html)

**The Double Occurrence of "the land had rest from war"**

Ellicott notes the difficulty of this phrase appearing both at Joshua 11:23 (where it naturally closes the conquest account) and here at 14:15. He suggests it may be connected to Caleb's final expulsion of the Anakim. Some modern scholars see this as evidence of editorial stitching in the book's composition. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-14.html)
